It Was Always Trying to Kill You

Every Lamborghini ever built arrived promising to be more civilized than the last one, and every Lamborghini ever built was lying. The Diablo SV is where that lie stopped being a problem and started being the product.

By Jolice Franklyn · 30 minute read

There is more engineering in the cheapest new car on sale today than there was in the entire 1995 Geneva Motor Show. A Chevrolet Spark will hold a lane, read a speed limit sign, brake for a cyclist you have not seen yet and tell you, gently, that you seem tired. At the other end of the price list a Bugatti will do 250 mph while keeping your coffee level. Both of those are triumphs. Both of them are also, in the specific sense that matters to anybody who has ever loved a car for irrational reasons, the same machine wearing different money.

Cars are still special. What has gone is character — the sense that a car has an opinion about you, and that the opinion is not necessarily favorable.

And for about forty years there was one company that had more of it than anybody. The loudest kid in the class, in clothing, in noise, in performance, in sheer wanting. Every time Lamborghini introduced something new, the press release swore it was more refined, more usable, more sensible than what came before. And every time, the car turned out to be a wild animal in a sports jacket that was still, quite openly, trying to kill you.

That was never the flaw in the product. That was the product.

Follow That

By the late 1980s the Countach had stopped being a car and become a piece of furniture in the collective imagination — the thing on ten million bedroom walls, the wedge that taught a whole generation what "fast" was supposed to look like. It had also been on sale since 1974, which in supercar years is roughly the reign of a medieval dynasty. Replacing it was not a product-planning exercise. It was a succession crisis.

Work on the replacement, internally Project 132, was authorized in June 1985 under the Mimran brothers, who had bought the wreckage of Lamborghini out of receivership a few years earlier and were, improbably, running it well. The brief was blunt: a minimum of 315 km/h (196 mph). Marcello Gandini, who had drawn both the Miura and the Countach, was given the shape. He worked the way he always had, from full-size drawings rather than sketches, and by April 1987 there was a running prototype painted an anonymous mousy gray with fake intakes stuck on it to confuse anybody with a long lens.

Then Detroit arrived.

The Chrysler Years, or How to Sand the Edges Off a Wedge

Chrysler bought Lamborghini on April 23, 1987 for about $25 million — roughly $70 million in 2026 money — and immediately put another $50 million of working capital in, which tells you exactly what state the place was in. Lee Iacocca's company now owned the most theatrical name in cars, and Lee Iacocca's design staff had opinions about Gandini's wedge.

What happened next depends entirely on who is telling it. One version, the one most often repeated, is that Chrysler's Detroit studio under Tom Gale was handed the car for a third major revision, softened every hard line Gandini had drawn, and left the Italian so exasperated that he took his original drawings elsewhere. The other version, told by Lamborghini's own technical director Luigi Marmiroli, is gentler: Detroit produced alternative clays, Iacocca then turned to Gandini and told him, in effect, you choose, you have the final say — and Gandini signed the production car, with a plaque on the right-hand side to prove it.

Both versions agree on the outcome. The Diablo that launched is rounder in the shoulders and calmer in the details than the car Gandini drew, and its interior — completely reworked by the Chrysler Design Center — is the part that period road testers would be rudest about for the next decade.

And the discarded design did go elsewhere. The front end of the Cizeta-Moroder V16T, the sixteen-cylinder oddity backed by the disco producer Giorgio Moroder, is Gandini's original Diablo nose. Claudio Zampolli did not like the rear, so he redid it himself. Here is the part that stings: the Cizeta was shown in Los Angeles in December 1988, which is thirteen months before the Diablo. Anybody who had seen one thought Lamborghini had copied the newcomer. It was the other way round, and by then it did not matter.

Speak of the Devil

The name did half the work before anybody saw the car. Diablo — the fighting bull bred by the Duke of Veragua that went nine rounds with the matador El Chicorro in Madrid in 1869, and, more to the point, a word that every human being on earth already understood. It sold the car in a single syllable. No badge in the industry has ever done more for less.

On January 21, 1990, in the Hôtel de Paris in Monte Carlo, they revealed it through red smoke with José Carreras singing. Iacocca said he had never seen a presentation like it. The price in America was $239,000, which is a shade over $613,000 in 2026 money, and the headline number was 202 mph.

Two hundred and two. In 1990, that was not a spec — it was a claim of territory.

About That 202

Here is where a good story has to survive a fact-check, and this one only just does.

Lamborghini type-approved the Diablo at 325 km/h — 202 mph — at Nardò, on its own runs, with its own drivers. Sandro Munari, the 1977 world rally champion who helped develop the car, is reported to have seen 340 km/h (211 mph) there. Those are the factory's numbers, produced by the factory, on the factory's day.

What is startling is that nobody outside the company appears to have checked. Auto Motor und Sport, the German magazine that had taken the Porsche 959, the Ferrari F40 and the Ruf CTR to Nardò in 1988 and published a top-speed table that defined the era, tested a Diablo in issue 5/1992 on a closed stretch of Italian autostrada. It recorded 0–100 km/h in 4.5 seconds and 0–200 km/h in 13.7 seconds. It did not record a maximum speed. It noted that the car kept pulling hard beyond 200 km/h, and that after the measured runs the brakes were finished.

Nobody else seems to have run one either. Which is remarkable, because the 200-mph war of the early 1990s turns out to have been fought almost entirely on paper.

When the Diablo launched, exactly two cars had been independently clocked past 200 mph: the Ruf CTR at 211 mph and the Porsche 959 S at 211 mph, both measured by Auto Motor und Sport at Nardò in 1988. Neither was really a catalog car — Ruf built somewhere around fifty CTRs, only 29 of them from bare chassis. The Ferrari F40, the car Lamborghini was explicitly gunning for, never once broke 200 mph under independent test: 199 mph for Sport Auto, 197 for Car and Driver, 196 for Road & Track.

The EB110 arrived in 1991, the XJ220 in 1992, the McLaren F1 in 1993. On the morning of January 21, 1990, Lamborghini could stand in Monte Carlo and say fastest production car in the world with a straight face, and the only thing anybody could do about it was wait.

What we are actually saying about 202 mph

It is a real figure, produced by real testing, at a real proving ground. It is also Lamborghini's own homologation number, and no independent instrumented run supporting it survives in the public record. Both of those things are true at once, and the second one does not make the first one a lie. It makes it a claim — which, in 1990, is what every top-speed number in this class was.

A Brief Note on the Company's Marital History

It is hard to keep up with who owned Lamborghini. The company has been in bed with more partners than a Vegas wedding chapel, and the Diablo lived through most of it.

Who owned Lamborghini while the Diablo was being drawn, built and killed
YearsOwnerReported price
1963–72Ferruccio Lamborghini—
1972–74Georges-Henri Rossetti (51 percent)not disclosed
1974–78René Leimer (the other 49 percent)not disclosed
1978–80Bankruptcy, then court receivership—
1980–87Jean-Claude and Patrick Mimranabout $3 million
1987–94Chrysler Corporationabout $25 million, plus $50 million working capital
1994–98MegaTech — Tommy Suharto and Mycom Setdco, later V'Powerabout $40 million

Read that table again with the Diablo in mind. The car was conceived by Frenchmen and Swiss money, styled by an Italian, redrawn by Detroit, launched by an American conglomerate, sold through the middle of its life by the son of an Indonesian president, facelifted by Audi and discontinued by Germans with a Murciélago to sell. The Diablo SV — the purest, angriest, most single-minded car in the whole family — was signed off during the Indonesian years, by a company that was building about two hundred cars annually and had recently had to cut its break-even point almost in half to survive.

That is the context nobody puts on the poster. In 1997, with the SV in full production, Lamborghini built 209 cars and turned a net profit of $120,000. Not $120 million. One hundred and twenty thousand dollars — about a quarter of what a single Diablo cost. The most excessive car on earth was being built by a company operating on the margins of a good week at a car dealership.

The Litter

There were a lot of Diablos, and several of them deserve their own piece. The short version, because the SV only makes sense standing next to its siblings:

Diablo VT, 1993

The one that grew up. A viscous-coupling center differential fed up to a quarter of the torque forward — the first all-wheel-drive V12 Lamborghini, and the reason a Diablo stopped being a weapon you had to physically wrestle in the wet. It also brought power steering across the range, which matters more than the four-wheel drive and gets mentioned a tenth as often. It weighed 1,625 kg (3,583 lb) dry, about 50 kg (110 lb) more than the rear-drive car, and it is the Diablo most people have actually driven.

Diablo SE30, 1993–94

The company's thirtieth birthday present to itself, and still the most extreme road Diablo. Carbon-fiber panels, Perspex side glass, no power windows, magnesium OZ wheels, cockpit-adjustable anti-roll bars, a fire suppression system and blue Alcantara everywhere. 525 hp and 1,451 kg (3,199 lb) dry — 125 kg (276 lb) lighter than a standard car. 150 built, at $211,000 apiece, which is about $489,000 today. It is now worth three times that, and we will come back to why.

SE30 Jota, 1995

Twenty-eight conversion kits — 12 fitted at Sant'Agata, 14 shipped to owners, 2 kept as spares. Twin ram intakes standing proud of the engine lid, a remapped ECU, a lighter crank, wilder cams, 595 hp. The rear-view mirror was deleted, on the entirely honest grounds that there was nothing left to see through it. It was built with GT racing in mind and it looks, even now, like something that escaped.

Diablo VT Roadster, 1995

A carbon-fiber targa panel you unclip by hand and stow on top of the engine cover, where it sits like a spoiler and announces to the entire street that you have taken the roof off. Cynical? Completely. Also the Diablo most owners say they enjoy most, and the one whose values have gone furthest in the last two years.

Diablo GT and GTR, 1999–2000

The end of the argument. A 5,992 cc engine, 575 hp, carbon body, stripped cabin, a fixed wing and a single exhaust exiting the middle of the tail. 83 GTs were assembled, and they were never sold legally in the United States. The GTR went further — 590 hp, race-only, carbon everywhere, a bonded roll cage — and was never legal anywhere you could buy fuel.

Enter the Super Veloce

Geneva, March 1995. Lamborghini put a Diablo on the stand with two extra brake ducts on the nose, an adjustable rear wing, a twin-scooped engine lid lifted from the Jota, 335-section rear tires, white instrument faces, Alcantara instead of leather and its own name written down the side in a script two feet long.

And then it did the genuinely strange thing.

It made the SV the cheapest Diablo you could buy. A roughly 10 percent cut against the standard rear-drive car; $229,900 in the United States when a VT Roadster stickered at $273,000. More power than any Diablo then on sale, less money than any Diablo then on sale. Under the new Indonesian ownership, with volumes on the floor, somebody in Sant'Agata worked out that the way to sell a Lamborghini was not to make it more sensible. It was to make it more of a Lamborghini and charge less for it.

How it got there is the part that makes purists wince. The SV is not a lightweight. It weighs 1,576 kg (3,474 lb) dry — exactly what a base Diablo weighs. There is no carbon, no Perspex, no deleted window motors. What there is, instead, is a deletion list: no viscous coupling, no front driveshafts, no front differential, no electronically adjustable Koni dampers. Lamborghini took the VT's clever bits out, turned the boost of the engine map and the exhaust up, and sold the result as the driver's car.

Which, infuriatingly, is exactly what it is.

The Diablo SV, the driver's car, most certainly is, for it is the best Lamborghini to be built since the original Miura SV. A period road test, 1997

Where SV Came From — and It Was Not 1974

The letters go back to one car. The Miura P400 SV, shown at the Geneva Motor Show in March 1971 — not 1974, a date that circulates widely and is wrong. Widened rear arches, nine-inch rear rims, separated engine and gearbox lubrication, revised rear geometry, a stiffened chassis, no headlight "eyelashes," and 385 hp at 7,850 rpm. Between 147 and 150 were built depending on whose registry you believe, with the last one not finally assembled until 1975.

It is the best Miura, by common consent, and it launched into almost total silence — because Lamborghini put the Countach prototype on the same stand, and nobody looked at anything else for the rest of the week. There is something very Lamborghini about the greatest version of the company's greatest car being upstaged, at birth, by the company.

What SV stands for is itself unsettled. Lamborghini today says Super Veloce, super fast, and that is the official line. Period Miura literature and the marque specialists say Spinto Veloce — spinto meaning pushed, or tuned. Both have a decent claim. Only one of them is on the company's website.

Which makes the Diablo the last rear-drive Super Veloce Lamborghini has built, thirty-one years and counting — and the only one after the Miura that asked its driver to sort out the back end personally.

What It Is Actually Like

Start with the door, because everybody does. You walk up to a car that is 2,040 mm (80.3 in) across — wider than a Range Rover of the same year — and 1,115 mm (43.9 in) tall, which is roughly belt height. The door swings up and forward. Then you have to get in, which involves sitting on the sill and posting yourself downward, and the whole sequence is designed, whether anybody meant it or not, to make you consider your decisions.

One contemporary tester called it "the most intimidating car made today, capable of invoking levels of trepidation not even a McLaren F1 or Ferrari F50 can induce." Then you fire it and discover the next thing: "it's absolutely deafening." Not loud at the top end. Loud at idle. The V12 is behind your shoulders with very little between you and it, and it snarls from the moment it catches.

The gear lever comes out of an exposed metal gate in the Ferrari tradition, right down to putting first gear on a dog-leg — down and to the left, outside the H that holds second through fifth. The clutch is heavy enough that owners who drive their cars in traffic will tell you about it unprompted. Tim Pitt, driving a 1998 SV for Motoring Research, described "the Diablo's weighty clutch and bicep-building gear shift" as "a culture shock" — and then noted, with the flat honesty that makes the line land, that "the rearward view is akin to peering through a very long letterbox."

What happens next is not what the reputation promises, and the honest reports keep saying so. The noise arrives first — Pitt heard a "deep, V8-like bellow" that "reverberates through your ribcage, then swells to furious mechanical crescendo," which is a fair description of a 60-degree V12 with no silencing worth the name. The steering, power-assisted since 1993 and therefore assisted on every SV ever built, is described by everyone who has driven one as sharp rather than heavy: "pointy steering makes it easy to place." The ride, of all things, is supple. Pitt found it "suited to British roads," which is the last sentence anybody expects in a Diablo review.

And then there is the other half, which is the half the car is famous for.

Given space, it will go round corners at speeds most cars won't reach on the straights — but you will be made to work for every inch of tarmac gained as you struggle to keep its massive bulk on line, operate the heavy gearbox and cope with its runaway performance. A period road test, 1997

That tester finished by saying you arrive "both mentally and physically exhausted," having gone "several rounds with the most tiring, stressful and demanding supercar money will currently buy." Peter Robinson, testing an SV at Croft for Wheels in 1996, got to the same place from a different direction: "Hugely powerful, incredibly noisy and tiring over any distance, the Diablo SV is also immensely entertaining." And then the sentence that should be printed on the sun visor: "For safety, use the brilliant brakes only in a straight line, otherwise there's a chance of the tail stepping rather quickly."

There is your car. Enormous grip, provided you have committed to the corner before you arrive in it. No stability control, no traction control, no ABS on anything built before the very end of production. Chris Harris, writing about an SV in 2012, put the ownership proposition in one sentence: "Physical, intimidating and very, very fast. There are no electronic safety nets, just the requirement of a prudent right foot to control those 335-section tyres."

The correction nobody makes

The unassisted-steering, arm-wrecking Diablo everybody talks about is the 1990–92 car. Power steering became standard across the range in 1993, two years before the SV existed. Every SV ever sold has it.

ABS is the opposite story and genuinely unsettled: sources put its arrival at either the 1998 model-year brake upgrade (Lucas) or the 1999 facelift (Kelsey-Hayes, with Dynamic Rear Proportioning). What is certain is that SVs built through at least 1997 have no anti-lock system at all, and that a period spec panel for a 1996 car lists servo assistance as yes and anti-lock as no.

Picking Holes Is Childishly Easy

The same tester who called it the best Lamborghini since the Miura SV also wrote this, and it is worth quoting in full because the last clause is the whole review: "the interior is a joke, the air conditioning scarcely works, jumping in and out is a nightmare and rearward visibility hardly exists, but with the Diablo SV they are as nothing."

Then the line that this entire article is built around:

It is not for posing on the Riviera, it is for blasting over the mountains, demanding and rewarding in a way that few this side of a Ferrari F40 would comprehend. A period road test, 1997

There were two kinds of Lamborghini buyer and the factory knew it perfectly well: the ones who wanted to be seen in the car, and the ones who wanted to drive it. With only the aging Diablo on the books, Lamborghini did the only thing available — it took the roof off for the first group and beefed up the engine and stripped out the interior for the second. The Roadster and the SV are the same commercial decision pointed in opposite directions.

How Quick Was It, Really?

Motor Trend puts the SV at 3.6 to 3.8 seconds to 60 mph, and about 12.2 seconds through the quarter mile at 118 to 126 mph. Those are the numbers to work from, and they are seriously quick — a Ferrari F50 costing three times as much went to 60 mph in 3.8.

Notice that they are ranges. A magazine's own instrumented run produces one elapsed time and one trap speed, not a spread of 8 mph, and the test indexes that catalog period road tests by publication carry six Diablo entries — a 1991 European coupe, a 1992 VT, a 1993 VT, a 1994 VT and two 2001 VT 6.0s — with no SV among them. The Diablo everybody remembers is the one the American buff books appear to have got to last.

The likely explanation is dull and sad: the SV arrived in the middle of the Mycom and V'Power interregnum, when American federalization and press-fleet support were both threadbare. The magazines tested what they were given, which was a VT, and then waited five years and tested the Audi-era 6.0.

Here is every published acceleration figure for the entire model run, which takes about ten seconds to read.

Two of those numbers are worth sitting with. The quickest Diablo on record is the last one — the 2001 VT 6.0 at 3.4 seconds, the car everybody writes off as the soft grand tourer. And the 1994 VT came in at 5.9 seconds, slower than a contemporary Corvette, which is almost certainly a story about how hard anybody is willing to launch somebody else's $250,000 car on a famously delicate single-plate clutch. Watch the trap speeds while you read the elapsed times: the traps barely move while the times swing by two and a half seconds. That gap is not the car. It is the first sixty feet.

Against the cars it was sold alongside, the SV needs no allowance made for it. Level with a 993 Turbo and an F50, clear of a 550 Maranello, a Viper GTS and an XJ220 — and cheaper than any of the Ferraris on the chart. The standing caveat applies to every number in this class from this decade: different magazines, different days, different surfaces. Jaguar claimed 3.6 seconds for the XJ220 and Road & Track measured 4.8, which is roughly how much daylight sat between a press release and a fifth wheel in 1995.

And the top speed is stranger still

Depending on the source, a Diablo SV will do 186, 199, 202, 204 or 207 mph. That spread is not sloppiness. It is gearing.

The SV was geared short, deliberately, for acceleration rather than a headline. A period road test spells out the trade: the 5.7-liter engine "would propel the Diablo to 338 kph (210 mph) were it not geared down to provide maximum acceleration," and the same article's spec panel lists the actual maximum as 300 kph — 186 mph. The Millennium Roadster of 2000 borrowed the SV's shorter final drive, 1:2.53 against the VT's 1:2.41, which is the same decision made again.

In other words: the fastest-sounding Lamborghini of the 1990s is, on paper, one of the slowest-topping ones, on purpose, because somebody at Sant'Agata decided that what a driver actually wants is the middle of third gear rather than a number to tell people at parties. It is the single most sensible engineering decision in this entire article, made by the least sensible company in the industry, on its least sensible car.

The Ones That Raced

In 1996 Lamborghini did something it had spent thirty-three years refusing to do. Ferruccio had famously wanted nothing to do with motorsport. His company, by then on its fourth set of owners, launched a one-make racing series.

The car was the Diablo SV-R, shown at Geneva in 1996: roughly 250 new components over the road car, 540 hp, 1,385 kg (3,053 lb), a fourteen-point chassis reinforcement, a roll cage, Brembo brakes, polycarbonate windows, the pop-up headlights deleted for weight and a plaque on each car reading Diablo SV modificata Racing. Reports of how many were built range from 25 to 34, which by now will not surprise you.

The series was the Philippe Charriol SuperSport Trophy — named, inevitably, for a watchmaker — and the first race ran on the undercard of the 1996 Le Mans 24 Hours, with five transporters delivering 28 cars. It was, and remains, the only single-make series in history run entirely on V12s.

It also turns out to have mattered. The Trophy was organized under Stéphane Ratel and used as a live laboratory for production-based regulations: professional-and-amateur driver pairings, driver grading, balance-of-performance adjustment. Those three ideas are now the load-bearing structure of every GT series on earth. As Motor Sport put it in 2021: "Without the Diablo Super Trophy in the mid-1990s, GT3 might never even have existed."

The wildest Lamborghini of the 1990s accidentally invented modern sports car racing. Nobody planned that either.

The Nissan Headlights, and the End

Volkswagen completed the purchase in July 1998, and at Paris that October the facelifted 1999 Diablo appeared with its pop-up headlights gone. In their place, under clear covers, sat fixed composite units licensed from the Nissan 300ZX.

The official justification is better night vision, less weight and better aerodynamics, all of which are true. The unofficial one is that you do not develop and homologate a new headlamp for a car whose replacement is already being drawn. An owner later demonstrated that the housing carries a Nissan marking, which Lamborghini had covered with a carbon-fiber lip — a detail so perfectly of its moment that it deserves a small plaque.

The 1999 SV got more than lights. Variable valve timing lifted it to 530 hp and 605 Nm (446 lb-ft), the torque peak moving down 400 rpm as it rose. The dashboard was replaced entirely, which finally made room for a passenger airbag. The structure went up about 15 percent in stiffness. ABS arrived. Forty-six kilograms came out. And the whole car became, measurably, better.

It also became less interesting, which is the standing tax on getting better.

The last SVs were finished in early 2000. Only the VT 6.0 carried on — Luc Donckerwolke's re-skin over Gandini's architecture, 550 hp, 337 built, and by every account the best-assembled Diablo of the lot. Forty-two 6.0 SE cars closed the book in 2001, available in gold or bronze and nothing else, because of course they were.

What a 1995 Supercar Actually Had

It is worth spelling out what "1990s technology" means in a car like this, because it is not what the phrase suggests.

There is no traction control and no stability control. There is no anti-lock braking. There are no driving modes, because there is nothing to mode. There is no launch control, no active aerodynamics, no adaptive damping — the SV specifically had the VT's adjustable Konis removed. The gearbox is a five-speed manual with an exposed metal gate, and the only thing between the engine's 510 hp and two 335-section rear tires is your right ankle.

What it does have, gloriously, is the wrong kind of technology. An Alpine head unit in the center console. A climate control panel with a small red digital readout of the sort last seen in a 1993 camcorder. Switchgear shared, unapologetically, with cars costing a twentieth as much. A dashboard clock by Breguet that cost about $10,000 as an option, which fifty people bought. And a cast alloy engine cover with the firing order for all twelve cylinders written on it, because somebody assumed the owner would need to know.

That is the actual character of nineties supercar engineering: enormous effort spent on the mechanical parts, and everything else bought in a hurry from whoever was answering the phone. The car has no opinion about what you are doing and no ability to intervene. It goes exactly where you point it, including off.

What They Cost Now

The Diablo spent two decades as the cheap way into a V12 Lamborghini, and the market has spent the last ten years correcting that with some force. Prices have roughly doubled over the decade; Hagerty has median condition-2 values up about 90 percent since 2019. In the early 2010s a usable VT or SV sat at £180,000–£250,000. A right-hand-drive SV is now a £550,000 retail car.

Then you adjust for inflation, and the story turns inside out.

In real money — 1990 dollars and 2026 dollars on the same footing — a base Diablo is still worth barely half what it cost. The VT is down roughly a third. The SV and the 6.0 have not appreciated at all in thirty years; they have broken even. Only the SE30 and the GT, the two that were rare and difficult from the start, have made anybody genuinely rich.

The much-quoted 90 percent surge since 2019 is not a bubble above the original price. It is a long climb back toward it.

Within the market, the sorting is brutal. A 21,000-mile SE30 made $741,000 in February 2026; an 8,000-mile one made $1,627,500 three weeks later at the same auction house. A 1,000-mile VT Roadster made $828,000 in August; a modified one with an unverified odometer made $319,000 in February. Four SVs failed to meet reserve between November 2025 and August 2026, and the ones that stalled were the high-mileage cars — 32,000, 46,000, 48,000 miles.

Which means the honest advice is the opposite of the headline. Diablos are not going up. Good Diablos are going up.

Does the SV command a premium over a VT?

Yes, but a smaller one than the badge suggests. Classic.com's benchmarks put the SV at $493,175 against the VT's $412,722 — about 20 percent, widening to roughly 40 percent for the 1999 facelift cars. That is not a rarity premium; roughly 350 SVs were built against about 530 VT coupes, which is not a dramatic difference. It is an analog-purity premium, the same force pushing manual Murciélagos to double the money of the paddle-shift cars.

And it is fragile. A well-kept VT 6.0 now out-values almost any SV, and a tired SV may not sell at all.

The Manual Gearbox Argument, Which the Diablo Wins By Not Playing

Look at what has happened to gated manuals. A manual Murciélago carries roughly double the value of an e-gear car — $408,475 against $195,930 on Classic.com's benchmarks, and the LP640 Roadster splits $863,875 against $342,228, a premium of over 150 percent. A manual F355 Berlinetta runs about 34 percent ahead of the F1 car. Aftermarket manual conversions of an F355 now benchmark higher than any factory manual F355 variant, which is the market shouting.

Every Diablo ever built is a gated manual. There was never a paddle option. The entire model line sits on the correct side of the single biggest value divide in modern collecting, by default, because the technology to do otherwise did not exist when it was made.

It is the largest, loudest, most famous supercar of which that is true.

Living With One

The reputation for financial terror is overdone, but only slightly. Service is annual, or every 6,750 miles. The clutch is the defining cost and wants replacing around 18,000 miles, which sounds ruinous until you find out that a Lamborghini dealer clutch is $3,000-plus for the part while a Valeo unit is a little over $1,000 — and that the Ferrari 550 Maranello clutch is directly interchangeable and wholesales around $800. Labor is the larger half of the bill and nobody publishes a number, which tells you something.

Known weak spots: the heavy clutch action on early cars, slave cylinder failures, suspension bushings, dampers, engine mounts. The real risk on any purchase is crash damage, which is why every specialist says the same thing about a pre-purchase inspection. Thin service history is normal rather than alarming — for most of the Diablo's life Britain had exactly one official Lamborghini dealer.

The thing that has genuinely changed is parts. Lamborghini Polo Storico, the factory's classic department, now supplies over 65 percent of the components across the Diablo range and issues certification. That single fact underpins the values more than any nostalgia cycle. A car you can actually get parts for is a car people will actually buy.

Why Anyone Would Want One Now

Because there is nothing else like it and there is not going to be.

A modern Lamborghini is a stupendous machine and it is also, in the ways that matter here, a supervised one. It will tighten its own line, meter its own torque, choose its own gear, hold its own nose up and hand you an experience that has already been edited for your safety. That is not a criticism. It is what makes a 1,000-horsepower car survivable, and the engineering behind it is genuinely astonishing.

But it is a conversation between you and a committee of processors, and the processors get the final word.

The Diablo SV gets no final word. It has a large, hot, extremely loud engine directly behind your head, a gearbox you have to be deliberate with, brakes you must use in a straight line, tires wide enough to plow a field and absolutely no interest in whether you are up to any of it. It is 2,040 mm wide and you will feel every millimeter of that on a British lane or a canyon road. It will go round a corner faster than most cars will go along a straight, and it will make you earn the entire distance.

The strangest part, and the part nobody warns you about, is that it is not actually undrivable. The honest modern reviews keep landing on the same surprise — the ride is supple, the steering is precise, the thing tracks straight, and driving one hard is less frightening than the folklore promised. Robinson's warning about the brakes was real, and so was his verdict: immensely entertaining. One period tester put it best, in a line that reads like a legal disclaimer and is actually a love letter: the SV is a challenge to drive hard and should only be driven that way within the safety of a test track, and though it tends to behave unreasonably well, it is not a car for faint hearts or for the inexperienced driver.

Tends to behave unreasonably well. That is the review. Not "it will kill you." Something more interesting: it might, and it would be your fault, and it is going to let you find out.

Verdict

The Diablo SV is the last of the big, mid-engined, take-it-or-leave-it supercars — a shape from 1985, a brief from 1971, an engine that traces to Giotto Bizzarrini's 1963 V12, sold by a company that changed hands three times while it was on the price list, built at a rate of about four cars a week by people who were not sure they would be employed the following spring.

It was the most powerful Diablo you could buy and the cheapest. It was called Super Veloce and it weighed the same as the standard car. Its top speed varies by 21 mph depending on which page you read, because it was geared to accelerate instead. Nobody ever tested it properly. It has no ABS, an interior assembled from a parts catalog, air conditioning that barely works, and a rear window through which you can see a letterbox-shaped slice of your own past.

And every single one of those facts is a reason to want it.

It is not for posing on the Riviera. It is for blasting over the mountains. The only sentence the Diablo SV ever needed

Cars are still special. This one is still dangerous, in the specific, old-fashioned, entirely voluntary way that we seem to have decided is no longer worth building. Thirty-one years later, nobody has made another Super Veloce that sends its power to only two wheels, and nobody is going to.

It was always trying to kill you. Turns out that was never the bug.
